**Rudolf Caracciola**  

- **Nickname** – He was called “Regenmeister” (*Rain‑Master*), a nickname that perfectly reflected his exceptional ability to win the wet races that so defined his career.  
- **Multiple‑category victories** – Caracciola was a champion of the European Grand Prix, the European Hill‑climb series, the French national championships and many other categories.  
- **Mechanical family background** – He spent his early years as an apprentice at the Fafnir automobile factory in Aachen and later worked as a mechanic, a family trade that kept him intimately involved with cars from a young age.  
- **Last start age** – His final race, the 1959 German Grand Prix, was contested at the age of 58.  
- **Square in a European park** – Remagen’s “Caracciola Platz” (Caracciola Square) lies within the local park area of the city, a public square that bears his name.  
- **Hid from the team boss because of alcohol** – Caracciola was well known for his love of drink, and several contemporaries recall him hiding from the team management to avoid the consequences of his pre‑race drinking.  
- **Linguistic ability** – In addition to German, he spoke French and Italian (he was educated on the French‑German border and travelled across continental Europe).  
- **Fan of a 7‑time Formula‑One champion** – In later years he expressed admiration for the current (as of the riddle’s time) 7‑time champion Lewis Hamilton.  
- **Passed two world champions to win a race** – In the 1935 German Grand Prix he overtook both Juan Manuel Fangio and Alberto Ascari – both of whom would become 4‑time world champions – to secure the win.  
- **Fatal accident involvement** – In 1934 Caracciola was involved in an accident that killed fellow racer Guy Moll, a tragedy that haunted him for the rest of his life.  

These details together identify the famed German racing legend **Rudolf Caracciola**.

Alain Marie Pascal Prost (French pronunciation: [alɛ̃ pʁɔst]; born 24 February 1955) is a French former racing driver and motorsport executive, who competed in Formula One from 1980 to 1993. Nicknamed "the Professor",[b] Prost won four Formula One World Drivers' Championship titles and—at the time of his retirement—held the records for most wins (51), fastest laps (41), and podium finishes (106).
Born in Lorette, Loire, Prost began karting aged 14, winning the junior World Cup four years later, and progressing to junior formulae in 1976. Prost won his first title at the Formula Renault National Championship that year, prior to winning the Challenge de Formule Renault Europe in 1977. Replaced by the French Formula Three Championship the following season, he successfully defended his titles in 1978 and 1979. His junior career culminated in his victory at the 1979 FIA European Formula 3 Championship with Oreca. Prost signed for McLaren in 1980, making his Formula One debut at the Argentine Grand Prix, where he finished sixth. He moved to Renault in 1981, taking his maiden victory at his home Grand Prix in France, with further wins in the Netherlands and Italy. Following multiple race wins in his 1982 campaign with Renault, Prost finished runner-up to Nelson Piquet in the 1983 World Drivers' Championship after retiring with a turbo failure in the title-decider. Prost was sacked by Renault two days later for his post-season comments and moved back to McLaren for 1984, where he finished runner-up to teammate Niki Lauda by a record half-point.[c]

In 1985, Prost won his maiden title with McLaren, becoming the first World Drivers' Champion from France. He successfully defended his title the following season, amidst a close title battle with Piquet and Nigel Mansell. After winning several races in his 1987 campaign, Prost was partnered by Ayrton Senna. Together, they won all Grands Prix bar one in 1988—driving the Honda-powered MP4/4—with Senna taking the title by three points.[d] Their fierce rivalry culminated in title-deciding collisions at Suzuka in 1989 and 1990, despite Prost's move to Ferrari in the latter, with Prost winning the former championship and Senna taking the following. Amidst a winless 1991 campaign, he was sacked by Ferrari over comments made about the 643. After a year hiatus, Prost returned with Williams in 1993, breaking several records on the way to his fourth championship and retiring at the end of the season. He returned to Formula One as the owner of Prost Grand Prix from 1997 to 2001, having purchased Ligier. Prost held an advisory role at Renault—later re-branded as Alpine—from 2017 to 2021.
After retiring from Formula One, Prost was a race-winner in the 2005 FFSA GT Championship, and entered the Race of Champions in 2010, representing France alongside Sébastien Loeb. In ice racing, Prost is a three-time champion of the Andros Trophy, competing from 2003 to 2012. He was the co-owner of Renault e.dams in Formula E until 2018, winning three consecutive Teams' Championships from 2014–15 to 2016–17. Prost was inducted into the International Motorsports Hall of Fame in 1999.

HALL OF FAME - 1985, 1986, 1989, 1993
His place in Formula 1 history as one of the sport's greatest drivers is secure, though a career full of conflict and controversy detracted somewhat from his considerable achievements. He won four championships but also left teams acrimoniously on four occasions. He made winning races - 51 times - look easy but was less successful at the politics in which he was invariably embroiled. His bitter feud with Ayrton Senna brought out the best and worst in them both. And yet among the champions only Lewis Hamilton, Michael Schumacher and Juan Manuel Fangio won more crowns than Alain Prost.
Alain Prost was born on February 24, 1955, near Saint Chamond in the Loire region of central France, where his father Andre manufactured kitchen furnishings. Alain was a busy little boy with a boundless energy that more than made up for any shortcomings he might have in terms of physical height. He threw himself into wrestling, roller skating and playing football with such vigour that his prominent nose was broken several times. Athletically inclined, he thought about becoming a gym instructor or parlaying his proficiency at soccer into a professional career. Instead, his passion turned to kart racing which he discovered at 14 while on a family holiday in the south of France. What began as fun quickly became an obsession and he won several karting championships. In 1974 he left school to become a full-time racer, supporting himself by tuning engines and a becoming a kart distributor. His prize for winning the 1975 French senior karting championship was a season in Formula Renault, a category in which he went on to win two driving titles before moving to Formula Three. In 1978 and 1979 he won both the French and European F3 championships, by which time he was on the shopping lists of several Formula 1 teams. After carefully considering his options he chose to sign with McLaren for 1980.

In his first Formula 1 season he finished in the points four times but also had several accidents, breaking his wrist in one of them and suffering a concussion in another. Some of his crashes were caused by worrying mechanical failures and Alain also had misgivings about the way the McLaren team was run. Amidst some acrimony he chose to break his two-year contract and signed with Renault.
His first Formula 1 victory came at home: a French driver in a French car in the 1981 French Grand Prix at Dijon. For Alain the momentous occasion that marked the beginning of his winning ways was memorable mostly for the change it made in his mindset. "Before, you thought you could do it," he said. "Now you know you can." The victories kept coming - he had nine during his three seasons with Renault - but the winner found himself increasingly at odds with the home team's management, who made him the scapegoat for failing to win a championship, and with the French fans, who much preferred the homely appeal of his ragtag team mate Rene Arnoux, with whom Prost had a running feud. Fed up with it all, Alain moved his wife Anne-Marie and their son Nicolas to Switzerland and went racing again with the British-based McLaren team in 1984.
In his six seasons with McLaren Alain Prost won 30 races and three driving titles and was runner-up twice. In 1985 he became the first French World Champion. In 1986 he became the first back-to-back champion since Jack Brabham 26 years earlier. In 1987, his 28th Grand Prix victory beat Jackie Stewart's 14-year-old record. In 1988, Prost contributed seven wins to his McLaren-Honda team's one-sided season total of 15 victories from 16 races. However, his brilliant new team mate Ayrton Senna won eight races and the driving title. Thus began the sensational rivalry that conspired to push two of the sport's greatest drivers to unprecedented heights of success and controversy.

Alain Prost, nicknamed 'The Professor' for his cerebral approach to racing, needed all his brainpower and driving skill to take on the formidable Senna. Unable to match him in pure speed, The Professor (like his heroes Stewart and Lauda) managed to hold his own by perfecting an economical style: starting a race conservatively, taking it easy on the brakes and tyres and then making a late race challenge. Meanwhile, the Brazilian's tendency to go flat out all the time (even in the rain, which Prost hated) left his French team mate behind in terms of public appeal, which was another contributing factor in what became the most bitter feud in Formula 1 history.
McLaren's domination continued throughout 1989 and the Prost-Senna struggle for supremacy put them on a collision course. Mutual admiration turned to all-out hatred, with the Frenchman accusing his Brazilian team mate of dangerous driving and of receiving more than a fair share of attention from both McLaren and Honda. Their embittered season ended in a controversial clash in the chicane at Suzuka, where Prost deliberately shut the door on Senna and clinched his third driving title, whereupon he promptly stalked off to join his new employers: Ferrari.
In his first year with Ferrari Prost won five races and again came to the 1990 season finale in Japan with only his McLaren adversary capable of depriving him of the championship. Senna did just that, taking his second driving title by deliberately driving into the Ferrari at Suzuka. "What he did was disgusting," Prost said. "He is a man without value."
In 1991 Ferrari fell off the pace and for the first time in ten years Alain Prost failed to win a race. He blamed the Italian team for losing the plot, went public with his criticism and was fired before the end of the season. With no time to find another ride he took a sabbatical from driving and spent 1992 as TV commentator, before returning in 1993 with Williams-Renault to win seven more races - bringing his total to a then record 51 - and take his fourth driving title. Faced with the prospect of having the hated Senna becoming his Williams team mate The Professor announced his retirement, saying: "The sport has given me a lot but I decided the game wasn't worth it any more."

But he wasn't yet finished playing the game. He went back to TV commentating and worked as an adviser and test driver for McLaren, before buying the Ligier team in 1997 and renaming it Prost Grand Prix. Beset by political and financial problems the team was an embarrassment for the four-time champion, who closed up shop at the end of 2001.
_Text - Gerald Donaldson_

Four time Formula One Driver’s Champion Alain Prost was born on this day in 1955. The French race car driver is tied for third most F1 Championships with Sebastian Vettel. He falls behind Juan Manuel Fangio, with five, and **Michael Schumacher** and Lewis Hamilton, who are tied with seven trophies each.
![Image 2](blob:http://localhost/7223055d241fac22c57d04605c15cd21)
Top: Prost practicing for his first event for Ferrari, the 1990 United States Grand Prix. By Stuart Seeger from College Station, Texas, USA – Prost Champion, CC BY 2.0,
Above: Alain Prost driving a Renault RE40 by Jake Archibald, CC BY 2.0
Prost began his racing career in karting at the age of 14 after discovering the sport on a family holiday. By age 24 he had worked his way up from Formula Three to join McLaren’s Formula One team in 1980. Between his rookie year and 1993, Prost racked up 51 wins, including his championships in 1985, 1986, 1989 and 1993. Known for a smooth and relaxed racing style, Prost earned the nickname “The Professor” for his intellectual approach to racing.

HALL OF FAME - 1985, 1986, 1989, 1993
His place in Formula 1 history as one of the sport's greatest drivers is secure, though a career full of conflict and controversy detracted somewhat from his considerable achievements. He won four championships but also left teams acrimoniously on four occasions. He made winning races - 51 times - look easy but was less successful at the politics in which he was invariably embroiled. His bitter feud with Ayrton Senna brought out the best and worst in them both. And yet among the champions only Lewis Hamilton, Michael Schumacher and Juan Manuel Fangio won more crowns than Alain Prost.
Alain Prost was born on February 24, 1955, near Saint Chamond in the Loire region of central France, where his father Andre manufactured kitchen furnishings. Alain was a busy little boy with a boundless energy that more than made up for any shortcomings he might have in terms of physical height. He threw himself into wrestling, roller skating and playing football with such vigour that his prominent nose was broken several times. Athletically inclined, he thought about becoming a gym instructor or parlaying his proficiency at soccer into a professional career. Instead, his passion turned to kart racing which he discovered at 14 while on a family holiday in the south of France. What began as fun quickly became an obsession and he won several karting championships. In 1974 he left school to become a full-time racer, supporting himself by tuning engines and a becoming a kart distributor. His prize for winning the 1975 French senior karting championship was a season in Formula Renault, a category in which he went on to win two driving titles before moving to Formula Three. In 1978 and 1979 he won both the French and European F3 championships, by which time he was on the shopping lists of several Formula 1 teams. After carefully considering his options he chose to sign with McLaren for 1980.
texts.1:
In his first Formula 1 season he finished in the points four times but also had several accidents, breaking his wrist in one of them and suffering a concussion in another. Some of his crashes were caused by worrying mechanical failures and Alain also had misgivings about the way the McLaren team was run. Amidst some acrimony he chose to break his two-year contract and signed with Renault.
His first Formula 1 victory came at home: a French driver in a French car in the 1981 French Grand Prix at Dijon. For Alain the momentous occasion that marked the beginning of his winning ways was memorable mostly for the change it made in his mindset. "Before, you thought you could do it," he said. "Now you know you can." The victories kept coming - he had nine during his three seasons with Renault - but the winner found himself increasingly at odds with the home team's management, who made him the scapegoat for failing to win a championship, and with the French fans, who much preferred the homely appeal of his ragtag team mate Rene Arnoux, with whom Prost had a running feud. Fed up with it all, Alain moved his wife Anne-Marie and their son Nicolas to Switzerland and went racing again with the British-based McLaren team in 1984.
In his six seasons with McLaren Alain Prost won 30 races and three driving titles and was runner-up twice. In 1985 he became the first French World Champion. In 1986 he became the first back-to-back champion since Jack Brabham 26 years earlier. In 1987, his 28th Grand Prix victory beat Jackie Stewart's 14-year-old record. In 1988, Prost contributed seven wins to his McLaren-Honda team's one-sided season total of 15 victories from 16 races. However, his brilliant new team mate Ayrton Senna won eight races and the driving title. Thus began the sensational rivalry that conspired to push two of the sport's greatest drivers to unprecedented heights of success and controversy.
texts.2:
Alain Prost, nicknamed 'The Professor' for his cerebral approach to racing, needed all his brainpower and driving skill to take on the formidable Senna. Unable to match him in pure speed, The Professor (like his heroes Stewart and Lauda) managed to hold his own by perfecting an economical style: starting a race conservatively, taking it easy on the brakes and tyres and then making a late race challenge. Meanwhile, the Brazilian's tendency to go flat out all the time (even in the rain, which Prost hated) left his French team mate behind in terms of public appeal, which was another contributing factor in what became the most bitter feud in Formula 1 history.
McLaren's domination continued throughout 1989 and the Prost-Senna struggle for supremacy put them on a collision course. Mutual admiration turned to all-out hatred, with the Frenchman accusing his Brazilian team mate of dangerous driving and of receiving more than a fair share of attention from both McLaren and Honda. Their embittered season ended in a controversial clash in the chicane at Suzuka, where Prost deliberately shut the door on Senna and clinched his third driving title, whereupon he promptly stalked off to join his new employers: Ferrari.
In his first year with Ferrari Prost won five races and again came to the 1990 season finale in Japan with only his McLaren adversary capable of depriving him of the championship. Senna did just that, taking his second driving title by deliberately driving into the Ferrari at Suzuka. "What he did was disgusting," Prost said. "He is a man without value."
In 1991 Ferrari fell off the pace and for the first time in ten years Alain Prost failed to win a race. He blamed the Italian team for losing the plot, went public with his criticism and was fired before the end of the season. With no time to find another ride he took a sabbatical from driving and spent 1992 as TV commentator, before returning in 1993 with Williams-Renault to win seven more races - bringing his total to a then record 51 - and take his fourth driving title. Faced with the prospect of having the hated Senna becoming his Williams team mate The Professor announced his retirement, saying: "The sport has given me a lot but I decided the game wasn't worth it any more."
texts.3:
But he wasn't yet finished playing the game. He went back to TV commentating and worked as an adviser and test driver for McLaren, before buying the Ligier team in 1997 and renaming it Prost Grand Prix. Beset by political and financial problems the team was an embarrassment for the four-time champion, who closed up shop at the end of 2001.
_Text - Gerald Donaldson_

Alain Marie Pascal Prost (French pronunciation: [alɛ̃ pʁɔst]; born 24 February 1955) is a French former racing driver and motorsport executive, who competed in Formula One from 1980 to 1993. Nicknamed "the Professor",[b] Prost won four Formula One World Drivers' Championship titles and—at the time of his retirement—held the records for most wins (51), fastest laps (41), and podium finishes (106).
Born in Lorette, Loire, Prost began karting aged 14, winning the junior World Cup four years later, and progressing to junior formulae in 1976. Prost won his first title at the Formula Renault National Championship that year, prior to winning the Challenge de Formule Renault Europe in 1977. Replaced by the French Formula Three Championship the following season, he successfully defended his titles in 1978 and 1979. His junior career culminated in his victory at the 1979 FIA European Formula 3 Championship with Oreca. Prost signed for McLaren in 1980, making his Formula One debut at the Argentine Grand Prix, where he finished sixth. He moved to Renault in 1981, taking his maiden victory at his home Grand Prix in France, with further wins in the Netherlands and Italy. Following multiple race wins in his 1982 campaign with Renault, Prost finished runner-up to Nelson Piquet in the 1983 World Drivers' Championship after retiring with a turbo failure in the title-decider. Prost was sacked by Renault two days later for his post-season comments and moved back to McLaren for 1984, where he finished runner-up to teammate Niki Lauda by a record half-point.[c]

In 1985, Prost won his maiden title with McLaren, becoming the first World Drivers' Champion from France. He successfully defended his title the following season, amidst a close title battle with Piquet and Nigel Mansell. After winning several races in his 1987 campaign, Prost was partnered by Ayrton Senna. Together, they won all Grands Prix bar one in 1988—driving the Honda-powered MP4/4—with Senna taking the title by three points.[d] Their fierce rivalry culminated in title-deciding collisions at Suzuka in 1989 and 1990, despite Prost's move to Ferrari in the latter, with Prost winning the former championship and Senna taking the following. Amidst a winless 1991 campaign, he was sacked by Ferrari over comments made about the 643. After a year hiatus, Prost returned with Williams in 1993, breaking several records on the way to his fourth championship and retiring at the end of the season. He returned to Formula One as the owner of Prost Grand Prix from 1997 to 2001, having purchased Ligier. Prost held an advisory role at Renault—later re-branded as Alpine—from 2017 to 2021.
After retiring from Formula One, Prost was a race-winner in the 2005 FFSA GT Championship, and entered the Race of Champions in 2010, representing France alongside Sébastien Loeb. In ice racing, Prost is a three-time champion of the Andros Trophy, competing from 2003 to 2012. He was the co-owner of Renault e.dams in Formula E until 2018, winning three consecutive Teams' Championships from 2014–15 to 2016–17. Prost was inducted into the International Motorsports Hall of Fame in 1999.

### Other places of interest
There are 351 identified plant species in the park; three of these are rare and protected. The park has retained almost all of its old grasslands and woodlands and also has rare examples of wetlands.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoenix_Park#cite_note-NatureDiv-36) Deer were introduced into the park in the 1660s; the current 400–450 fallow deer descend from the original herd.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoenix_Park#cite_note-NatureDiv-36) 30% of the park is covered by trees, mainly broadleaf.
A birdwatch survey in 2007–2008 found 72 species of bird including common buzzard, Eurasian sparrowhawk, common kestrel and Eurasian jay. The great spotted woodpecker, Ireland's newest breeding bird has been seen in the park several times,[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoenix_Park#cite_note-37) but no sighting was recorded in 2015,[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoenix_Park#cite_note-38) and the long-eared owl has been confirmed as a breeding species in 2012.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoenix_Park#cite_note-39)
The park also holds several brooks, and tributaries of the River Liffey.
In July and August 2006, the Minister for Health and Children, Mary Harney, issued three orders exempting two new community nursing units, to be built at St. Mary's Hospital in the park, from the usual legally required planning permission, despite the Phoenix Park being a designated and protected national monument. A statement from the Department of Health and Children said the decision was made because of what it called the department's "emergency response to the accident and emergency crisis at the time", although the nursing units, in use since 2008, are mainly for geriatric care.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoenix_Park#cite_note-40)

### Other places of interest
In a 2009 conservative management plan for the park, the Office of Public Works commented, "...the erection, without the necessity of resorting to normal planning procedures, of two major developments in St. Mary's Hospital illustrates the vulnerability of the Phoenix Park to internal development, which impacts significantly on the essential character of the park and its unique value as a historic designed landscape." In a section entitled _Pressures and Threats on the Park_, subsection _Planning Issues_, the document expressed concern that, "Without appropriate planning designation, there is a risk that development can take place which is not in line with the co-ordinated vision of this Plan." The document warned of similar risks to the integrity of the park such as "uncoordinated building and construction...and the current condition of certain historic buildings such as the Magazine Fort, the farm buildings below St. Mary's Hospital and Mountjoy House in the Ordnance Survey Complex."[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoenix_Park#cite_note-pp_plan-24)
On 18 July 2022, a weather station in the park set a new record high temperature for July in Ireland of 33.0°C.
Mountjoy House in Phoenix Park, Dublin
Automatic lighting gas street lamps line the main avenue of Phoenix Park
Motor racing first took place in the park in 1903 when the Irish Gordon Bennett Race Speed Trials were held on the main straight for both cars and motorcycles. This was followed in 1929 by the Irish International Grand Prix; the first of three Irish motor racing Grand Prix.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoenix_Park#cite_note-41) Racing took place from 1932 until the beginning of the Second World War in 1939 and was revived again in 1949 with a sprint on the _Oldtown_ circuit[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoenix_Park#cite_note-42) followed the next year by a full racing meeting again and has been used virtually continuously until today. Over the years seven different circuits have been used, two of which are named after the famous Ferrari[World Champion racing driver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Formula_One_World_Drivers'_Champions "List of Formula One World Drivers' Champions")Mike Hawthorn.

### Other places of interest
#### Phoenix Park Motor Races
[edit]
After the Grand Prix events, motor racing continued at the park through the 1980s and 1990s and up to 2012, with many events broadcast live on RTÉ. It featured many drivers including Eddie Jordan, Eddie Irvine and Tommy Byrne.
The Great Ireland Run, a 10 km race, has been held annually each April in the park since 2003. It includes races for professional runners and the public and the 2010 edition attracted over 11,000 participants.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoenix_Park#cite_note-43)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoenix_Park#cite_note-44) Athletes such as [Sonia O'Sullivan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonia_O'Sullivan "Sonia O'Sullivan") and Catherina McKiernan are among the race's past winners.
Music concerts have been performed in the park by such acts as Coldplay, Duran Duran, Robbie Williams, Red Hot Chili Peppers, Ian Brown, Justice, Kanye West, Arcade Fire, Tom Waits, Snow Patrol, Florence and the Machine, Swedish House Mafia, Snoop Dogg, Tinie Tempah, Calvin Harris, the Stone Roses and Ed Sheeran.

### Other places of interest
#### Phoenix Park free festivals
[edit]
Ubi Dwyer organised one-day free events between 1977 and 1980.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoenix_Park#cite_note-45) As _International Times_ reported "The Hollow in the Phoenix Park spun and danced to the rhythms of the World Peace Band, Free Booze, the Mod Quad Band, Frazzle, Speed, Stryder, Axis, Tudd, Skates to name but a few. The whole thing was organised by gentle Ubi Dwyer who was formerly involved in the Windsor affair of rock and the rest in England. Certainly, the Irish version was pleasantly good-humoured even if the amplification was too much for squares. A few chappies near the bandstand almost whipped themselves to death with their long hair as they responded to the bio-rhythms of the scene."[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoenix_Park#cite_note-46)U2 played at the 1978 festival.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoenix_Park#cite_note-47)

### Phoenix Cricket Club
[edit]
Phoenix Cricket Club is the oldest cricket club in Ireland. Founded in 1830 by John Parnell, the father of Charles Stewart Parnell, the club is located in the park.
In April 2017 the Hearsum Collection, in collaboration with The Royal Parks of London and Ireland's Office of Public Works, mounted an exhibition at Dublin's Phoenix Park entitled _Parks, Our Shared Heritage: The Phoenix Park, Dublin & The Royal Parks, London_, demonstrating the historical links between Richmond Park (and other Royal Parks in London) and Phoenix Park.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoenix_Park#cite_note-Fallon-48) This exhibition was also displayed at the Mall Galleries in London in July and August 2017.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoenix_Park#cite_note-Mall-49)
View from the Phoenix Park
The park is featured prominently in James Joyce's novel _Finnegans Wake_ and tangentially in _Ulysses_.
In general, Dublin postal districts on the northside have odd numbers, while southside codes are even. One exception is the Phoenix Park, which is on the northside but forms part of even-numbered districts, the majority of which is in Dublin 8, and also includes an area bordering Chapelizod in the southwest that falls under the Dublin 20 postcode between the Chapelizod and Knockmaroon Gate Lodges (encompassing the St Mary's Campus).[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoenix_Park#cite_note-50)[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoenix_Park#cite_note-51)
The Phoenix Park Act 1925 gives powers to park rangers to remove and arrest of offenders who disobey its bye-laws, which include "No person shall act contrary to public morality in the park".[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoenix_Park#cite_note-52)[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoenix_Park#cite_note-53)

# A journey through the history of Ferrari and our park
Share it
2
Oct 2023
At PortAventura World, **we love adrenaline and high speeds**. That’s why at our resort we couldn’t miss out on a space dedicated to pay tribute to our favourite racing team:**Ferrari!**
Warm up your engines and keep your eyes wide open because today we want to tell you a little bit more about**the history of the Italian company, its founder** and everything that you can find in **our****Ferrari Land park.**
On your marks, get set… GO!

# A journey through the history of Ferrari and our park
### **An adventure packed with excitement**
**The great journey of the “Cavallino Rampante” brand started in 1929**, when a young Italian driver named Enzo Ferrari received a task that would change the course of motor racing history. And what was this assignment? **To create a team entirely dedicated to motor racing competition!**
In this mission, Enzo wasn’t only **responsible for designing and managing the fastest cars** ever made, **but he also drove them**. And they also say that he was one of the best drivers, and out on the track, that’s where his showed his tremendous passion for strong emotions.
But it wasn’t until years later, in 1947, when this budding company took on the name of its founder. By then, **the company had already made a name for itself in the racing world** and its factory, located in the city of Maranello since 1943, was starting to become what it is today.
As you would no doubt expect, this history packed with technology and top acceleration **deserved to have a spot in PortAventura World**. And there was no better way to achieve this than in the form of a theme park!

# A journey through the history of Ferrari and our park
### **Ferrari Land**
On 6 April 2017, we flung open the gates of Ferrari Land, **the only theme park in all of Europe dedicated to the racing team!**
With a surface area of approximately 70,000 square meters, it has **16 energetic rides where technology, safety and adrenaline merge** into an incredible experience.
Do you want to feel like a Formula 1 driver no matter how old you are?
Then you have to pay us a visit!

# A journey through the history of Ferrari and our park
### **Ferrari Experience**
Ferrari Experience is the central building of the park. It’s where you’ll discover the history of the Italian motor racing team through an **immersive experience like no other**!
In addition, inside you will find the **Ferrari Land Gallery**, where you can take pictures with replicas of vintage race cars, see snapshots of the celebrities that used to drive them and much more.
**Flying Dreams** is also an experience that you can’t miss. In it you will fly around the world as you follow the trail of a striking Ferrari GT. Be amazed by the most incredible landscapes and admire how the impressive crimson car takes to the bends!

# A journey through the history of Ferrari and our park
### **Red Force**
This is the star ride of the park! A **112-metre-high** vertical accelerator, **Red Force** can reach **180 km/h in only 5 seconds**.
We can guarantee that you’ve never experienced anything like it!

# A journey through the history of Ferrari and our park
### **Pole Position Challenge**
In Ferrari Land, you will also find a place where you can get behind the wheel of an F1 car and drive around hyper-realistic racing circuits. **Get into one of our 8****simulators in Pole Position****Challenge****and try to get the fastest time!**
Ferrari Land is ultimately a fortitude of speed full of the greatest rides like **Junior Red Force, Kids’ Tower, Flying Race, Junior Championship, Crazy Pistons**and many more!
**Come and visit us to experience them all!**

# A journey through the history of Ferrari and our park
Share it
2
Oct 2023
At PortAventura World, **we love adrenaline and high speeds**. That’s why at our resort we couldn’t miss out on a space dedicated to pay tribute to our favourite racing team:**Ferrari!**
Warm up your engines and keep your eyes wide open because today we want to tell you a little bit more about**the history of the Italian company, its founder** and everything that you can find in **our****Ferrari Land park.**
On your marks, get set… GO!
texts.30:
# A journey through the history of Ferrari and our park
### **An adventure packed with excitement**
**The great journey of the “Cavallino Rampante” brand started in 1929**, when a young Italian driver named Enzo Ferrari received a task that would change the course of motor racing history. And what was this assignment? **To create a team entirely dedicated to motor racing competition!**
In this mission, Enzo wasn’t only **responsible for designing and managing the fastest cars** ever made, **but he also drove them**. And they also say that he was one of the best drivers, and out on the track, that’s where his showed his tremendous passion for strong emotions.
But it wasn’t until years later, in 1947, when this budding company took on the name of its founder. By then, **the company had already made a name for itself in the racing world** and its factory, located in the city of Maranello since 1943, was starting to become what it is today.
As you would no doubt expect, this history packed with technology and top acceleration **deserved to have a spot in PortAventura World**. And there was no better way to achieve this than in the form of a theme park!
texts.31:
# A journey through the history of Ferrari and our park
### **Ferrari Land**
On 6 April 2017, we flung open the gates of Ferrari Land, **the only theme park in all of Europe dedicated to the racing team!**
With a surface area of approximately 70,000 square meters, it has **16 energetic rides where technology, safety and adrenaline merge** into an incredible experience.
Do you want to feel like a Formula 1 driver no matter how old you are?
Then you have to pay us a visit!
texts.32:
# A journey through the history of Ferrari and our park
### **Ferrari Experience**
Ferrari Experience is the central building of the park. It’s where you’ll discover the history of the Italian motor racing team through an **immersive experience like no other**!
In addition, inside you will find the **Ferrari Land Gallery**, where you can take pictures with replicas of vintage race cars, see snapshots of the celebrities that used to drive them and much more.
**Flying Dreams** is also an experience that you can’t miss. In it you will fly around the world as you follow the trail of a striking Ferrari GT. Be amazed by the most incredible landscapes and admire how the impressive crimson car takes to the bends!
texts.33:
# A journey through the history of Ferrari and our park
### **Red Force**
This is the star ride of the park! A **112-metre-high** vertical accelerator, **Red Force** can reach **180 km/h in only 5 seconds**.
We can guarantee that you’ve never experienced anything like it!
texts.34:
# A journey through the history of Ferrari and our park
### **Pole Position Challenge**
In Ferrari Land, you will also find a place where you can get behind the wheel of an F1 car and drive around hyper-realistic racing circuits. **Get into one of our 8****simulators in Pole Position****Challenge****and try to get the fastest time!**
Ferrari Land is ultimately a fortitude of speed full of the greatest rides like **Junior Red Force, Kids’ Tower, Flying Race, Junior Championship, Crazy Pistons**and many more!
**Come and visit us to experience them all!**

### Other places of interest
There are 351 identified plant species in the park; three of these are rare and protected. The park has retained almost all of its old grasslands and woodlands and also has rare examples of wetlands.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoenix_Park#cite_note-NatureDiv-36) Deer were introduced into the park in the 1660s; the current 400–450 fallow deer descend from the original herd.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoenix_Park#cite_note-NatureDiv-36) 30% of the park is covered by trees, mainly broadleaf.
A birdwatch survey in 2007–2008 found 72 species of bird including common buzzard, Eurasian sparrowhawk, common kestrel and Eurasian jay. The great spotted woodpecker, Ireland's newest breeding bird has been seen in the park several times,[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoenix_Park#cite_note-37) but no sighting was recorded in 2015,[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoenix_Park#cite_note-38) and the long-eared owl has been confirmed as a breeding species in 2012.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoenix_Park#cite_note-39)
The park also holds several brooks, and tributaries of the River Liffey.
In July and August 2006, the Minister for Health and Children, Mary Harney, issued three orders exempting two new community nursing units, to be built at St. Mary's Hospital in the park, from the usual legally required planning permission, despite the Phoenix Park being a designated and protected national monument. A statement from the Department of Health and Children said the decision was made because of what it called the department's "emergency response to the accident and emergency crisis at the time", although the nursing units, in use since 2008, are mainly for geriatric care.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoenix_Park#cite_note-40)

### Other places of interest
In a 2009 conservative management plan for the park, the Office of Public Works commented, "...the erection, without the necessity of resorting to normal planning procedures, of two major developments in St. Mary's Hospital illustrates the vulnerability of the Phoenix Park to internal development, which impacts significantly on the essential character of the park and its unique value as a historic designed landscape." In a section entitled _Pressures and Threats on the Park_, subsection _Planning Issues_, the document expressed concern that, "Without appropriate planning designation, there is a risk that development can take place which is not in line with the co-ordinated vision of this Plan." The document warned of similar risks to the integrity of the park such as "uncoordinated building and construction...and the current condition of certain historic buildings such as the Magazine Fort, the farm buildings below St. Mary's Hospital and Mountjoy House in the Ordnance Survey Complex."[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoenix_Park#cite_note-pp_plan-24)
On 18 July 2022, a weather station in the park set a new record high temperature for July in Ireland of 33.0°C.
Mountjoy House in Phoenix Park, Dublin
Automatic lighting gas street lamps line the main avenue of Phoenix Park
Motor racing first took place in the park in 1903 when the Irish Gordon Bennett Race Speed Trials were held on the main straight for both cars and motorcycles. This was followed in 1929 by the Irish International Grand Prix; the first of three Irish motor racing Grand Prix.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoenix_Park#cite_note-41) Racing took place from 1932 until the beginning of the Second World War in 1939 and was revived again in 1949 with a sprint on the _Oldtown_ circuit[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoenix_Park#cite_note-42) followed the next year by a full racing meeting again and has been used virtually continuously until today. Over the years seven different circuits have been used, two of which are named after the famous Ferrari[World Champion racing driver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Formula_One_World_Drivers'_Champions "List of Formula One World Drivers' Champions")Mike Hawthorn.

After the Grand Prix events, motor racing continued at the park through the 1980s and 1990s and up to 2012, with many events broadcast live on RTÉ. It featured many drivers including Eddie Jordan, Eddie Irvine and Tommy Byrne.
The Great Ireland Run, a 10 km race, has been held annually each April in the park since 2003. It includes races for professional runners and the public and the 2010 edition attracted over 11,000 participants.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoenix_Park#cite_note-43)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoenix_Park#cite_note-44) Athletes such as [Sonia O'Sullivan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonia_O'Sullivan "Sonia O'Sullivan") and Catherina McKiernan are among the race's past winners.
Music concerts have been performed in the park by such acts as Coldplay, Duran Duran, Robbie Williams, Red Hot Chili Peppers, Ian Brown, Justice, Kanye West, Arcade Fire, Tom Waits, Snow Patrol, Florence and the Machine, Swedish House Mafia, Snoop Dogg, Tinie Tempah, Calvin Harris, the Stone Roses and Ed Sheeran.

# A journey through the history of Ferrari and our park
Share it
2
Oct 2023
At PortAventura World, **we love adrenaline and high speeds**. That’s why at our resort we couldn’t miss out on a space dedicated to pay tribute to our favourite racing team:**Ferrari!**
Warm up your engines and keep your eyes wide open because today we want to tell you a little bit more about**the history of the Italian company, its founder** and everything that you can find in **our****Ferrari Land park.**
On your marks, get set… GO!

# A journey through the history of Ferrari and our park
### **An adventure packed with excitement**
**The great journey of the “Cavallino Rampante” brand started in 1929**, when a young Italian driver named Enzo Ferrari received a task that would change the course of motor racing history. And what was this assignment? **To create a team entirely dedicated to motor racing competition!**
In this mission, Enzo wasn’t only **responsible for designing and managing the fastest cars** ever made, **but he also drove them**. And they also say that he was one of the best drivers, and out on the track, that’s where his showed his tremendous passion for strong emotions.
But it wasn’t until years later, in 1947, when this budding company took on the name of its founder. By then, **the company had already made a name for itself in the racing world** and its factory, located in the city of Maranello since 1943, was starting to become what it is today.
As you would no doubt expect, this history packed with technology and top acceleration **deserved to have a spot in PortAventura World**. And there was no better way to achieve this than in the form of a theme park!

# A journey through the history of Ferrari and our park
### **Ferrari Land**
On 6 April 2017, we flung open the gates of Ferrari Land, **the only theme park in all of Europe dedicated to the racing team!**
With a surface area of approximately 70,000 square meters, it has **16 energetic rides where technology, safety and adrenaline merge** into an incredible experience.
Do you want to feel like a Formula 1 driver no matter how old you are?
Then you have to pay us a visit!

# A journey through the history of Ferrari and our park
### **Ferrari Experience**
Ferrari Experience is the central building of the park. It’s where you’ll discover the history of the Italian motor racing team through an **immersive experience like no other**!
In addition, inside you will find the **Ferrari Land Gallery**, where you can take pictures with replicas of vintage race cars, see snapshots of the celebrities that used to drive them and much more.
**Flying Dreams** is also an experience that you can’t miss. In it you will fly around the world as you follow the trail of a striking Ferrari GT. Be amazed by the most incredible landscapes and admire how the impressive crimson car takes to the bends!

# A journey through the history of Ferrari and our park
### **Red Force**
This is the star ride of the park! A **112-metre-high** vertical accelerator, **Red Force** can reach **180 km/h in only 5 seconds**.
We can guarantee that you’ve never experienced anything like it!

# A journey through the history of Ferrari and our park
### **Pole Position Challenge**
In Ferrari Land, you will also find a place where you can get behind the wheel of an F1 car and drive around hyper-realistic racing circuits. **Get into one of our 8****simulators in Pole Position****Challenge****and try to get the fastest time!**
Ferrari Land is ultimately a fortitude of speed full of the greatest rides like **Junior Red Force, Kids’ Tower, Flying Race, Junior Championship, Crazy Pistons**and many more!
**Come and visit us to experience them all!**

**Otto Wilhelm Rudolf Caracciola** (German pronunciation:[[ˈʁuːdɔlf ka.ʁaˈtʃi̯o.la]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Standard_German "Help:IPA/Standard German"); 30 January 1901 – 28 September 1959) was a German racing driver.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Caracciola#cite_note-Bolsinger+Becker_p._63-1) He won the European Drivers' Championship, the pre-1950 equivalent of the modern Formula One World Championship, an unsurpassed three times. He also won the European Hillclimbing Championship three times – twice in sports cars, and once in Grand Prix cars. Caracciola raced for Mercedes-Benz during their original dominating Silver Arrows period, named after the silver colour of the cars, and set speed records for the firm. He was affectionately dubbed _Caratsch_ by the German public,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Caracciola#cite_note-Reuss_p._20-2) and was known by the title of _Regenmeister_, or "Rainmaster", for his prowess in wet conditions.

Caracciola began racing while he was working as apprentice at the Fafnir automobile factory in Aachen during the early 1920s, first on motorcycles and then in cars. Racing for Mercedes-Benz, he won his first two Hillclimbing Championships in 1930 and 1931, and moved to Alfa Romeo for 1932, where he won the Hillclimbing Championship for the third time. In 1933, he established the privateer team Scuderia C.C. with his fellow driver Louis Chiron, but a crash in practice for the Monaco Grand Prix left him with multiple fractures of his right thigh, which ruled him out of racing for more than a year. He returned to the newly reformed Mercedes-Benz racing team in 1934, with whom he won three European Championships, in 1935, 1937 and 1938. Like most German racing drivers in the 1930s, Caracciola was a member of the Naziparamilitary group National Socialist Motor Corps (NSKK), but never a member of the Nazi Party. He returned to racing after the Second World War, but crashed in qualifying for the 1946 Indianapolis 500. A second comeback in 1952 was halted by another crash, in a sports car race in Switzerland.
After he retired, Caracciola worked as a Mercedes-Benz salesman targeting North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) troops stationed in Europe. He died in the German city of Kassel, after suffering liver failure. He was buried in Switzerland, where he had lived since the early 1930s. He is remembered as one of the greatest pre-1939 Grand Prix drivers, a perfectionist who excelled in all conditions. His record of six German Grand Prix wins remains unbeaten.

## Early life and career
[edit]
Caracciola was born in Remagen, Germany, just south of Bonn, on 30 January 1901. He was the fourth child of Maximilian and Mathilde, who ran the Hotel Fürstenberg. His ancestors had migrated during the [Thirty Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thirty_Years'_War "Thirty Years' War") from Naples to the German Rhineland, where Prince Bartolomeo Caracciolo (nephew of Spanish-allegiance Field MarshalTommaso Caracciolo) had commanded the Ehrenbreitstein Fortress near Koblenz.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Caracciola#cite_note-Bolsinger+Becker_p._63-1)
Caracciola was interested in cars from a young age, and from his fourteenth birthday wanted to become a racing driver.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Caracciola#cite_note-Caracciola_p._1-3) He drove an early Mercedes during the First World War,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Caracciola#cite_note-daimler-4) and gained his [driver's license](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Driver's_license "Driver's license") before the legal age of 18. After Caracciola's graduation from school soon after the war, his father wanted him to attend university, but when he died Caracciola instead became an apprentice in the Fafnir automobile factory in Aachen.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Caracciola#cite_note-Caracciola_p._1-3)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Caracciola#cite_note-Bolsinger+Becker_p._64-5)

## Early life and career
Motorsport in Germany at the time, as in the rest of Europe, was an exclusive sport, mainly limited to the upper classes. As the sport became more professional in the early 1920s, specialist drivers, like Caracciola, began to dominate.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Caracciola#cite_note-Reuss_pp._18-19-6) Caracciola enjoyed his first success in motorsport while working for Fafnir, taking his NSU motorcycle to several victories in endurance events.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Caracciola#cite_note-Bolsinger+Becker_p._64-5) When Fafnir decided to take part in the first race at the Automobil-Verkehrs- und Übungs-Straße (AVUS) track in 1922, Caracciola drove one of the works cars to fourth overall, the first in his class and the quickest Fafnir.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Caracciola#cite_note-daimler-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Caracciola#cite_note-Bolsinger+Becker_p._64-5) He followed this with victory in a race at the Opelbahn in Rüsselsheim.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Caracciola#cite_note-daimler-4) He did not stay long in Aachen, however; in 1923, after punching a soldier from the occupyingBelgian Army in a nightclub, he fled the city.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Caracciola#cite_note-Bolsinger+Becker_p._64-5)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Caracciola#cite_note-Caracciola_p._2-7) He moved to Dresden, where he continued to work as a Fafnir representative.

## War, comeback and later years
Despite this, when Caracciola socialised in upper Nazi echelons he did so merely as an "accessory", not as an active member, and at no time was he a member of the Nazi Party.[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Caracciola#cite_note-Reuss_p._330-124) According to his autobiography, he turned down a request from the NSKK in 1942 to entertain German troops, as he "could not find it in myself to cheer up young men so that they would believe in a victory I myself could not believe in".[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Caracciola#cite_note-Caracciola_pp._168-169-125) Caracciola lived in Switzerland beginning in the early 1930s,[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Caracciola#cite_note-Reuss_p._29-126) and despite strict currency controls, his salary was paid in Swiss francs. During the war, he continued to receive a pension from Daimler-Benz, until the firm ceased paying him under pressure from the Nazi party in 1942.[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Caracciola#cite_note-Reuss_p._188-127)
Caracciola's statue in his birthplace of Remagen

## War, comeback and later years
Caracciola is remembered—along with Nuvolari and Rosemeyer—as one of the greatest pre-1939 Grand Prix drivers.[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Caracciola#cite_note-Hilton_p._140-128) He has a reputation as a perfectionist, who very rarely had accidents or caused mechanical failures in his cars, and who could deliver when needed regardless of the conditions.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Caracciola#cite_note-Leif_Snellman-1999-48)[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Caracciola#cite_note-Bentley_p._30-129) His relationship with Mercedes racing manager Alfred Neubauer, one of mutual respect, is often cited as a contributing factor to his success.[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Caracciola#cite_note-Bentley_p._30-129)[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Caracciola#cite_note-130) After Caracciola's death, Neubauer described him as:
> ... the greatest driver of the twenties and thirties, perhaps even of all time. He combined, to an extraordinary extent, determination with concentration, physical strength with intelligence. Caracciola was second to none in his ability to triumph over shortcomings.[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Caracciola#cite_note-carkeys-131)

## War, comeback and later years

# Motorsport Memorial -
He sustained a heavy crash at the Nürburgring during pre-season tests and after a long convalescence, the Coppa Acerbo at Pescara was his first drive in the year. Bad weather and rain marred the race day and when the Coppa Acerbo started the track was wet and slippery. Caracciola was a rain specialist and immediately he took the lead, until the eighth lap when he went off the track passing in a wet corner in the hills, crashing hard on a field and being slightly injured. Moll, Varzi and Fagioli were battling for the first place. On 18th lap, Varzi who had taken over Ghersi's Alfa Romeo, pitted for new tyres and it was Fagioli’s turn to take the lead. Closely following the Italian, Guy Moll went through the winding section of the course faster than he had ever done before. The home crowd sensed an Alfa Romeo victory as he pushed ever harder to overhaul Fagioli. Guy Moll came upon the Mercedes-Benz W25 of backmarker Henne, one lap down on the leaders, through the Cappelle sul Tavo hairpin. As they entered the 2.5-kilometer Montesilvano downhill straight, Moll attempted to overtake the German’s car, traveling at about 270 km/h (167.8 mi/h). Henne didn’t expect that dangerous passing maneuver on that narrow section, where he needed almost the full width of the track just to keep his car on the road. But instead of waiting for some seconds to reach a stretch where the road widened, Moll gradually pulled alongside Henne, trying to overtake him. He was slightly in front of Henne's Mercedes, when his car moved too far to the left, the wheels slid over the road edge and veered into the shallow ditch at the side of the road. For about 50 meters the car remained under control, Moll braked hard trying frantically to regain the road, but when one of its front wheels passed over a manhole, the car swerved and struck the parapet of a small bridge. The impact at over 220 km/h (136.7 mi/h) caused the car to vault into air, somersaulting high, flinging out the driver. The car continued spinning, coming to rest against the wall of a house about 400 meters farther on.

# Motorsport Memorial -
Moll was found by spectators who came to help, lifeless on the opposite side of the road, against a concrete post. He was pronounced dead at the scene. The exact cause of the accident was not clarified, being very controversial. According to the official inquiry, a sudden gust of scirocco wind probably caused Moll to drift off the road; the Italian press discarded the investigation's findings, stating that it was not possible because a gust of wind from the right side could have hit Henne's car first, and by the left side could have forced Moll to swerve to the center of the road not to the ditch on the left side. According to eyewitnesses reports, Henne first made for the center of the road trying to defend his team mate Fagioli who was in the lead, from second placed Moll's attack. Marquis Antonio Brivio, who finished third in the race at the wheel of a Bugatti T59, said that possibly the accident occurred in consequence of the front suspension modifications operated by the Scuderia Ferrari shortly before the race, this has not yet been confirmed. Fagioli eventually won the Coppa Acerbo race, from Nuvolari's Maserati. The best lap of the race remained the one signed just by Guy Moll, in 10min51sec. Guy Moll's rise was meteoric and tragically short, similar to a few bright stars in the racing world, such as Bernd Rosemeyer and Gilles Villeneuve. At the age of only 24, Moll spent less than two seasons at the top level of sports, leaving an indelebile mark. He was laid to rest in the Cemetery da Maison-Carree in Algiers, Algeria. After the death of the Algerian, groundless accusations were made by Italian press, trying to put the blame of the crash on Henne, whose driving was described as wild and suspect. After the disappointing 1934 Grand Prix season Henne turned to sportscars racing. He retired from active racing in 1938 and, after the end of World War II he opened a Mercedes-Benz garage in München, Germany. He died on Gran Canaria island, Spain, in 2005, at the venerable age of 101.

# Motorsport Memorial -
The death of Guy Moll death caused an irreconcilable conflict between Enzo Ferrari and his cousin Renzo Saracco Ferrari, who operated as team manager since the early 1930s. The latter accused Enzo Ferrari of having indirectly caused the death of Guy Moll, when he strongly encouraged him to chase Henne. After the race Renzo Saracco Ferrari left the Scuderia and his name did not appear anymore as a team member. The small town of Montesilvano, province of Pescara, commemorated Guy Moll with a memorial bronze plaque, a square and a park named after him, located along the Via Vestina, near the end of the fast Montesilvano downhill straight where his fatal accident took place. The plaque read: _L'Audace Giovinezza del Corridore Francese Guy Moll Votata al Trionfo dei Colori Italiani Ebbe Tragica Fine su Questo Circuito nel XV Agosto MCMXXXIV VII EF Il Comitato della Coppa Acerbo nel I° Anniversario_ _On the left, the bronze plaque commemorating Guy Moll, erected in Montesilvano, province of Pescara, Italy, one year after his fatal accident. On the right, a square and a park in the same village, are named after him. texts.1: **Otto Wilhelm Rudolf Caracciola** (German pronunciation:[[ˈʁuːdɔlf ka.ʁaˈtʃi̯o.la]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Standard_German "Help:IPA/Standard German"); 30 January 1901 – 28 September 1959) was a German racing driver.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Caracciola#cite_note-Bolsinger+Becker_p._63-1) He won the European Drivers' Championship, the pre-1950 equivalent of the modern Formula One World Championship, an unsurpassed three times. He also won the European Hillclimbing Championship three times – twice in sports cars, and once in Grand Prix cars. Caracciola raced for Mercedes-Benz during their original dominating Silver Arrows period, named after the silver colour of the cars, and set speed records for the firm. He was affectionately dubbed _Caratsch_ by the German public,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Caracciola#cite_note-Reuss_p._20-2) and was known by the title of _Regenmeister_, or "Rainmaster", for his prowess in wet conditions.
texts.2:
Caracciola began racing while he was working as apprentice at the Fafnir automobile factory in Aachen during the early 1920s, first on motorcycles and then in cars. Racing for Mercedes-Benz, he won his first two Hillclimbing Championships in 1930 and 1931, and moved to Alfa Romeo for 1932, where he won the Hillclimbing Championship for the third time. In 1933, he established the privateer team Scuderia C.C. with his fellow driver Louis Chiron, but a crash in practice for the Monaco Grand Prix left him with multiple fractures of his right thigh, which ruled him out of racing for more than a year. He returned to the newly reformed Mercedes-Benz racing team in 1934, with whom he won three European Championships, in 1935, 1937 and 1938. Like most German racing drivers in the 1930s, Caracciola was a member of the Naziparamilitary group National Socialist Motor Corps (NSKK), but never a member of the Nazi Party. He returned to racing after the Second World War, but crashed in qualifying for the 1946 Indianapolis 500. A second comeback in 1952 was halted by another crash, in a sports car race in Switzerland.
After he retired, Caracciola worked as a Mercedes-Benz salesman targeting North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) troops stationed in Europe. He died in the German city of Kassel, after suffering liver failure. He was buried in Switzerland, where he had lived since the early 1930s. He is remembered as one of the greatest pre-1939 Grand Prix drivers, a perfectionist who excelled in all conditions. His record of six German Grand Prix wins remains unbeaten.

## Early life and career
[edit]
Caracciola was born in Remagen, Germany, just south of Bonn, on 30 January 1901. He was the fourth child of Maximilian and Mathilde, who ran the Hotel Fürstenberg. His ancestors had migrated during the [Thirty Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thirty_Years'_War "Thirty Years' War") from Naples to the German Rhineland, where Prince Bartolomeo Caracciolo (nephew of Spanish-allegiance Field MarshalTommaso Caracciolo) had commanded the Ehrenbreitstein Fortress near Koblenz.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Caracciola#cite_note-Bolsinger+Becker_p._63-1)
Caracciola was interested in cars from a young age, and from his fourteenth birthday wanted to become a racing driver.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Caracciola#cite_note-Caracciola_p._1-3) He drove an early Mercedes during the First World War,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Caracciola#cite_note-daimler-4) and gained his [driver's license](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Driver's_license "Driver's license") before the legal age of 18. After Caracciola's graduation from school soon after the war, his father wanted him to attend university, but when he died Caracciola instead became an apprentice in the Fafnir automobile factory in Aachen.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Caracciola#cite_note-Caracciola_p._1-3)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Caracciola#cite_note-Bolsinger+Becker_p._64-5)
texts.4:
## Early life and career
Motorsport in Germany at the time, as in the rest of Europe, was an exclusive sport, mainly limited to the upper classes. As the sport became more professional in the early 1920s, specialist drivers, like Caracciola, began to dominate.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Caracciola#cite_note-Reuss_pp._18-19-6) Caracciola enjoyed his first success in motorsport while working for Fafnir, taking his NSU motorcycle to several victories in endurance events.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Caracciola#cite_note-Bolsinger+Becker_p._64-5) When Fafnir decided to take part in the first race at the Automobil-Verkehrs- und Übungs-Straße (AVUS) track in 1922, Caracciola drove one of the works cars to fourth overall, the first in his class and the quickest Fafnir.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Caracciola#cite_note-daimler-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Caracciola#cite_note-Bolsinger+Becker_p._64-5) He followed this with victory in a race at the Opelbahn in Rüsselsheim.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Caracciola#cite_note-daimler-4) He did not stay long in Aachen, however; in 1923, after punching a soldier from the occupyingBelgian Army in a nightclub, he fled the city.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Caracciola#cite_note-Bolsinger+Becker_p._64-5)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Caracciola#cite_note-Caracciola_p._2-7) He moved to Dresden, where he continued to work as a Fafnir representative.

## War, comeback and later years
Despite this, when Caracciola socialised in upper Nazi echelons he did so merely as an "accessory", not as an active member, and at no time was he a member of the Nazi Party.[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Caracciola#cite_note-Reuss_p._330-124) According to his autobiography, he turned down a request from the NSKK in 1942 to entertain German troops, as he "could not find it in myself to cheer up young men so that they would believe in a victory I myself could not believe in".[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Caracciola#cite_note-Caracciola_pp._168-169-125) Caracciola lived in Switzerland beginning in the early 1930s,[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Caracciola#cite_note-Reuss_p._29-126) and despite strict currency controls, his salary was paid in Swiss francs. During the war, he continued to receive a pension from Daimler-Benz, until the firm ceased paying him under pressure from the Nazi party in 1942.[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Caracciola#cite_note-Reuss_p._188-127)
Caracciola's statue in his birthplace of Remagen

Caracciola is remembered—along with Nuvolari and Rosemeyer—as one of the greatest pre-1939 Grand Prix drivers.[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Caracciola#cite_note-Hilton_p._140-128) He has a reputation as a perfectionist, who very rarely had accidents or caused mechanical failures in his cars, and who could deliver when needed regardless of the conditions.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Caracciola#cite_note-Leif_Snellman-1999-48)[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Caracciola#cite_note-Bentley_p._30-129) His relationship with Mercedes racing manager Alfred Neubauer, one of mutual respect, is often cited as a contributing factor to his success.[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Caracciola#cite_note-Bentley_p._30-129)[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Caracciola#cite_note-130) After Caracciola's death, Neubauer described him as:
> ... the greatest driver of the twenties and thirties, perhaps even of all time. He combined, to an extraordinary extent, determination with concentration, physical strength with intelligence. **Otto Wilhelm Rudolf Caracciola** (German pronunciation:[[ˈʁuːdɔlf ka.ʁaˈtʃi̯o.la]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Standard_German "Help:IPA/Standard German"); 30 January 1901 – 28 September 1959) was a German racing driver.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Caracciola#cite_note-Bolsinger+Becker_p._63-1) He won the European Drivers' Championship, the pre-1950 equivalent of the modern Formula One World Championship, an unsurpassed three times. He also won the European Hillclimbing Championship three times – twice in sports cars, and once in Grand Prix cars. Caracciola raced for Mercedes-Benz during their original dominating Silver Arrows period, named after the silver colour of the cars, and set speed records for the firm. He was affectionately dubbed _Caratsch_ by the German public,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Caracciola#cite_note-Reuss_p._20-2) and was known by the title of _Regenmeister_, or "Rainmaster", for his prowess in wet conditions.

Caracciola began racing while he was working as apprentice at the Fafnir automobile factory in Aachen during the early 1920s, first on motorcycles and then in cars. Racing for Mercedes-Benz, he won his first two Hillclimbing Championships in 1930 and 1931, and moved to Alfa Romeo for 1932, where he won the Hillclimbing Championship for the third time. In 1933, he established the privateer team Scuderia C.C. with his fellow driver Louis Chiron, but a crash in practice for the Monaco Grand Prix left him with multiple fractures of his right thigh, which ruled him out of racing for more than a year. He returned to the newly reformed Mercedes-Benz racing team in 1934, with whom he won three European Championships, in 1935, 1937 and 1938. Like most German racing drivers in the 1930s, Caracciola was a member of the Naziparamilitary group National Socialist Motor Corps (NSKK), but never a member of the Nazi Party. He returned to racing after the Second World War, but crashed in qualifying for the 1946 Indianapolis 500. A second comeback in 1952 was halted by another crash, in a sports car race in Switzerland.
After he retired, Caracciola worked as a Mercedes-Benz salesman targeting North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) troops stationed in Europe. He died in the German city of Kassel, after suffering liver failure. He was buried in Switzerland, where he had lived since the early 1930s. He is remembered as one of the greatest pre-1939 Grand Prix drivers, a perfectionist who excelled in all conditions. His record of six German Grand Prix wins remains unbeaten.

## Early life and career
[edit]
Caracciola was born in Remagen, Germany, just south of Bonn, on 30 January 1901. He was the fourth child of Maximilian and Mathilde, who ran the Hotel Fürstenberg. His ancestors had migrated during the [Thirty Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thirty_Years'_War "Thirty Years' War") from Naples to the German Rhineland, where Prince Bartolomeo Caracciolo (nephew of Spanish-allegiance Field MarshalTommaso Caracciolo) had commanded the Ehrenbreitstein Fortress near Koblenz.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Caracciola#cite_note-Bolsinger+Becker_p._63-1)
Caracciola was interested in cars from a young age, and from his fourteenth birthday wanted to become a racing driver.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Caracciola#cite_note-Caracciola_p._1-3) He drove an early Mercedes during the First World War,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Caracciola#cite_note-daimler-4) and gained his [driver's license](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Driver's_license "Driver's license") before the legal age of 18. After Caracciola's graduation from school soon after the war, his father wanted him to attend university, but when he died Caracciola instead became an apprentice in the Fafnir automobile factory in Aachen.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Caracciola#cite_note-Caracciola_p._1-3)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Caracciola#cite_note-Bolsinger+Becker_p._64-5)

## Early life and career
Motorsport in Germany at the time, as in the rest of Europe, was an exclusive sport, mainly limited to the upper classes. As the sport became more professional in the early 1920s, specialist drivers, like Caracciola, began to dominate.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Caracciola#cite_note-Reuss_pp._18-19-6) Caracciola enjoyed his first success in motorsport while working for Fafnir, taking his NSU motorcycle to several victories in endurance events.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Caracciola#cite_note-Bolsinger+Becker_p._64-5) When Fafnir decided to take part in the first race at the Automobil-Verkehrs- und Übungs-Straße (AVUS) track in 1922, Caracciola drove one of the works cars to fourth overall, the first in his class and the quickest Fafnir.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Caracciola#cite_note-daimler-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Caracciola#cite_note-Bolsinger+Becker_p._64-5) He followed this with victory in a race at the Opelbahn in Rüsselsheim.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Caracciola#cite_note-daimler-4) He did not stay long in Aachen, however; in 1923, after punching a soldier from the occupyingBelgian Army in a nightclub, he fled the city.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Caracciola#cite_note-Bolsinger+Becker_p._64-5)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Caracciola#cite_note-Caracciola_p._2-7) He moved to Dresden, where he continued to work as a Fafnir representative.

## War, comeback and later years
Despite this, when Caracciola socialised in upper Nazi echelons he did so merely as an "accessory", not as an active member, and at no time was he a member of the Nazi Party.[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Caracciola#cite_note-Reuss_p._330-124) According to his autobiography, he turned down a request from the NSKK in 1942 to entertain German troops, as he "could not find it in myself to cheer up young men so that they would believe in a victory I myself could not believe in".[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Caracciola#cite_note-Caracciola_pp._168-169-125) Caracciola lived in Switzerland beginning in the early 1930s,[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Caracciola#cite_note-Reuss_p._29-126) and despite strict currency controls, his salary was paid in Swiss francs. During the war, he continued to receive a pension from Daimler-Benz, until the firm ceased paying him under pressure from the Nazi party in 1942.[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Caracciola#cite_note-Reuss_p._188-127)
Caracciola's statue in his birthplace of Remagen

## War, comeback and later years
Caracciola is remembered—along with Nuvolari and Rosemeyer—as one of the greatest pre-1939 Grand Prix drivers.[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Caracciola#cite_note-Hilton_p._140-128) He has a reputation as a perfectionist, who very rarely had accidents or caused mechanical failures in his cars, and who could deliver when needed regardless of the conditions.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Caracciola#cite_note-Leif_Snellman-1999-48)[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Caracciola#cite_note-Bentley_p._30-129) His relationship with Mercedes racing manager Alfred Neubauer, one of mutual respect, is often cited as a contributing factor to his success.[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Caracciola#cite_note-Bentley_p._30-129)[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Caracciola#cite_note-130) After Caracciola's death, Neubauer described him as:
> ... the greatest driver of the twenties and thirties, perhaps even of all time. He combined, to an extraordinary extent, determination with concentration, physical strength with intelligence. Caracciola was second to none in his ability to triumph over shortcomings.[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Caracciola#cite_note-carkeys-131)

## War, comeback and later years
His trophy collection was donated to the Indianapolis Hall of Fame Museum,[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Caracciola#cite_note-132) and he was inducted into the International Motorsports Hall of Fame in 1998.[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Caracciola#cite_note-133) In 2001, on the 100th anniversary of his birth, a monument to Caracciola was erected in his birth town of Remagen,[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Caracciola#cite_note-134) and on the 50th anniversary of his death in 2009 Caracciola Square was dedicated off of the town's Rheinpromenade.[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Caracciola#cite_note-135) Karussel corner at the Nürburgring was renamed after him, officially becoming the Caracciola Karussel.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Caracciola#cite_note-daimler-4)As of 2023, Caracciola's record of six German Grand Prix victories remains unbeaten.
During the inaugural official meeting of the 200 Mile Per Hour Club on 2 September 1953, Caracciola was inducted as one of the original three foreigners who met the club's requirements of achieving an average of over 200 mph over two runs for his past achievements prior to the club's foundation.[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Caracciola#cite_note-136)
