**John Michael Hawthorn** (10 April 1929 – 22 January 1959) was a British racing driver who competed in Formula One from 1952 to 1958. Hawthorn won the [Formula One World Drivers' Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Formula_One_World_Drivers'_Championship "Formula One World Drivers' Championship") in 1958 with Ferrari, and won three Grands Prix across seven seasons. In endurance racing, Hawthorn won both the 24 Hours of Le Mans and the 12 Hours of Sebring in 1955 with Jaguar.
In 1958, Hawthorn became the first of 11 British Formula One World Champions, beating Stirling Moss to the title by one point. He announced his retirement upon his triumph, having been profoundly affected by the death of his teammate and friend Peter Collins two months earlier during the German Grand Prix. Three months after retiring, Hawthorn died in a road accident in Guildford, driving his Jaguar 3.4 Litre. The Hawthorn Memorial Trophy was established in his honour by the RAC in 1959, being awarded to the most successful British, or Commonwealth, driver in Formula One each year.
Hawthorn was born in the town of Mexborough, West Riding of Yorkshire, England, to Leslie and Winifred (née Symonds) Hawthorn,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-2) and educated at Ardingly College, West Sussex, followed by studies at Chelsea technical college and an apprenticeship with a commercial vehicle manufacturer.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-Skilleter-3) His father owned the Tourist Trophy Garage in Farnham, franchised to supply and service several high performance brands, including Jaguar and Ferrari.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-MikeHawthorntributesite-4) His father raced motorcycles and supported his son's racing career; when he died in a road accident in 1954, Mike Hawthorn inherited the business.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-5)

Hawthorn made his competition debut on 2 September 1950 in his 1934 Riley Ulster Imp, KV 9475, winning the 1,100 cc sports car class at the Brighton Speed Trials.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-6) In 1951, driving a 1+1⁄2-litre T.T. Riley, he entered the _Motor Sport_Brooklands Memorial Trophy, a season-long contest run at Goodwood, winning it by one point.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-7) He also won the Ulster Trophy Handicap at Dundrod and the Leinster Trophy at Wicklow that year.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-8)
By 1952, Hawthorn had switched to single-seaters and during that season won his first race in a Formula TwoCooper-Bristol T20 at Goodwood. Further successes followed which brought him to the attention of Enzo Ferrari, who offered him a works drive. He made his Formula One debut at the 1952 Grote Prijs van Belgie on the legendary Circuit de Spa-Francorchamps, finishing in fourth place. By the end of the season, he had already secured his first podium, with a third place at the RAC British Grand Prix[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-9) and a brace of fourths driving a Cooper.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-f1-fansite.com-10)

At Scuderia Ferrari for the 1953 season, Hawthorn immediately showed his worth with victory, at his ninth attempt, in the French Grand Prix at Reims, outmanoeuvring Juan Manuel Fangio in what became dubbed 'the race of the century' with the top four drivers finishing within five seconds of each other after 60 laps.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-11) This and two other podium finishes helped him end the season fourth overall.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-ReferenceA-12) He also won the BRDC International Trophy[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-formula2.net-13) and the Ulster Trophy[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-14) as well as the 24 Heures de Spa Francorchamps with Ferrari teammate Giuseppe Farina.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-15)
Hawthorn's liability for conscription (National Service) was brought up in the House of Commons.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-16) In a crash during the Gran Premio di Siracusa Hawthorn suffered serious burns,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-Skilleter-3) but finished the year with three seconds and then victory in the season finale in Spain, placing him third in the Drivers' Championship.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-ReferenceB-17) Following the death of his father, Hawthorn left Ferrari to race for Tony Vandervell's Vanwall team, as he needed to spend more time at the family garage he had inherited,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-Skilleter-3) but after two races returned to Ferrari.

#### 24 Hours of Le Mans
Hawthorn rejoined the Ferrari factory team in 1957, and soon became friends with Peter Collins, a fellow Englishman and Ferrari team driver. During the 1957 and 1958 racing seasons, the two Englishmen became engaged in a fierce rivalry with Luigi Musso, another Ferrari driver, for prize money.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-grandprix.com-24)
Hawthorn driving his Ferrari to third in the Gran Premio de la Republica Argentina

### 1958 World Champion
[edit]
Hawthorn won the 1958 Formula One Championship despite achieving only one win, against four by Moss. Hawthorn won the 1958 French Grand Prix at Reims, in which Musso was fatally injured while in second place. Leading easily in the 1958 Monaco Grand Prix at half distance, his 246 engine blew,[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-25) while at Monza he was a minute ahead of Tony Brooks when his clutch forced him to slow to second place.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-26)
Hawthorn benefited greatly from the gentlemanliness of Moss, as demonstrated at the 1958 Portuguese Grand Prix at Porto. Hawthorn was disqualified for bump starting his stalled car downhill in the opposite direction, on the way to a second-place finish. Moss interceded on Hawthorn's behalf and the decision was ultimately reversed.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-ReferenceC-27) After a pit stop midway through that race, Hawthorn accelerated back through the field to gain an extra point for fastest lap. Moss had failed to respond, possibly doubting Hawthorn could lap so fast with damaged drum brakes.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-ReferenceC-27) This extra world championship point plus the second place points contributed to Hawthorn winning the championship with a season total just one more than that of Moss.

### 1958 World Champion
In the final race, the 1958 Moroccan Grand Prix, Hawthorn drove a conservative tactical race aiming to stay ahead of Moss's Vanwall teammates. Brooks's car broke while narrowly leading Hawthorn, and Stuart Lewis-Evans in the third Vanwall crashed after a desperate attempt to move through the field and challenge Hawthorn running third; Evans later died of burns. In the last laps, second-placed Phil Hill slowed and waved Hawthorn through to gain enough points to take the Championship; the first ever to be won by an English driver.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-Skilleter-3)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-28) Hawthorn's total of just one win in his title winning season means that Hawthorn currently jointly holds the Formula One record for the fewest number of Grand Prix wins by an eventual drivers' champion during a title winning season along with Keke Rosberg (who also scored one win in his subsequent 1982 title winning season)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-29)
After winning the title, Hawthorn immediately announced his retirement from Formula One. He began a series of books for children featuring not only the wholly fictional Carlotti, but also himself and other drivers of the day ('Stirling nipped past me at the hairpin', and so on). The first, published in 1958, was _Carlotti Joins the Team_, and a second was published in 1959 called _Carlotti Takes the Wheel_.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-30) Due to his death, the series did not continue.
Hawthorn was noted for wearing a bow tie when racing;[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-31)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-32) to the French, he became known as 'Le Papillon' (The Butterfly).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-Skilleter-3)

## Rivalry with Luigi Musso
[edit]
Fiamma Breschi, Musso's girlfriend at the time of his death, revealed the nature of Musso's rivalry with Hawthorn and Collins in a television documentary, _The Secret Life of Enzo Ferrari_, many years after the death of Hawthorn. Breschi recalled that the antagonism between Musso and the two English drivers encouraged all three to take more risks: "The Englishmen (Hawthorn and Collins) had an agreement", she says. "Whichever of them won, they would share the winnings equally. It was the two of them against Luigi, who was not part of the agreement. Strength comes in numbers, and they were united against him. This antagonism was actually favourable rather than damaging to Ferrari. The faster the drivers went, the more likely it was that a Ferrari would win." Breschi related that Musso was in debt at the time of his death, and the money for winning the 1958 French Grand Prix (traditionally the largest monetary prize of the season), was all-important to him.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-grandprix.com-24)
After visiting the mortally injured Musso in hospital, Breschi returned to her hotel, where she and the rest of the Ferrari team were informed by the team manager that Musso had died. Within thirty days Collins too was dead, and the following January, Hawthorn. Breschi could not suppress a feeling of release: "I had hated them both", she said, "first because I was aware of certain facts that were not right, and also because when I came out of the hospital and went back to the hotel, I found them in the square outside the hotel, laughing and playing a game of football with an empty beer can. So when they died, too, it was liberating for me. Otherwise I would have had unpleasant feelings towards them forever. This way I could find a sense of peace."[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-grandprix.com-24)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-33)

## Rivalry with Luigi Musso
After leaving school in the summer of 1946, Hawthorn started serving his apprenticeship with Dennis Bros of Guildford in Surrey. He used his 1939 250cc OHV Triumph to get there each day regularly racing Jack Kinghorn on his Triumph Thunderbird on the infamous A31 [Hog's Back](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hog's_Back "Hog's Back") between Farnham where his father's garage was located and the Guildford A3 factory where they both worked. Hawthorn never married, but fathered a son, Arnaud Michael Delaunay born 1954, with Jacqueline Delaunay, whom he met in Reims after winning the French Grand Prix in 1953. He was engaged at the time of his death to the fashion model Jean Howarth, who later married another racing driver, Innes Ireland, in 1993.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-Nixon-34)
A 1959 Jaguar 3.4 Mk.1
On 22 January 1959, only three months after his retirement, Hawthorn died in a car accident on the A3 Guildford bypass near Onslow Village, while driving his comprehensively modified 1958 Jaguar 3.4-litre saloon (now known as the 3.4 Mk 1) VDU 881 to London. While the circumstances of the accident are well documented, the precise cause remains unknown.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-35)

## hawthornes
[[](https://www.instagram.com/swallowsracing) swallowsracing 9,067 We recently had the pleasure of heading up to Jaguar Classic to be a part of the Le Mans ’88 Inside Out event. Hearing untold stories and first-hand experiences from an incredible board of speakers. Andy Wallace – winner of the ’88 Le Mans in the TWR Jaguar XJR-9. Mike Wilds – Rival works Nissan. Eddie Hinkley – Race engineer. Rod Benoist – Chief mechanic. Richard West – TWR marketing Director. Hosted by Wayne Scott – Editor of Jaguar Enthusiast Magazine. Now, as far as lineups go, this is as strong as they come. Upon arrival the car park was filled with a huge array of the best Jaguar has to offer, 1 of only 2 UK produced Italian Racing Red XKR-S GT’s took prime position right outside the front door whilst a French Racing Blue XFR-S estate parked quietly out on the outskirts of the venue. There was also 2 F-Pace SVR Le Mans 1988 editions hidden in plain sight, quite fitting for the nature of the event. Let’s head inside! Immediately over to the left, the actual race winning Jaguar XJR-9 from the ’88 Le Mans race. A stunning Silverstone Green Jaguar XJ220 and the beautiful Jagaur XJR-15 R9R. To the right, a dark green Jaguar C-Type, lightweight Jagaur E-Type and a D-Type. As well as 2 F-Types, one being a 70th anniversary edition. Moving away from the cars, the talk began with brief introductions before falling into deep conversation about the legendary ’88 Le Mans. First hand recollections from the cockpit of the XJR9 by driver Andy Wallce, stories so vivid it were as if we were there with him. Over the next few hours we delved into all things technical, on track and off track, battles, pit lane drama and so much more. Time flew by as we were transported back to ’88 and before we knew it the talk was over. After a brief walk around the incredible facilities at Jaguar Classic it was time to jump in the car and head back down south.

**John Michael Hawthorn** (10 April 1929 – 22 January 1959) was a British racing driver who competed in Formula One from 1952 to 1958. Hawthorn won the [Formula One World Drivers' Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Formula_One_World_Drivers'_Championship "Formula One World Drivers' Championship") in 1958 with Ferrari, and won three Grands Prix across seven seasons. In endurance racing, Hawthorn won both the 24 Hours of Le Mans and the 12 Hours of Sebring in 1955 with Jaguar.
In 1958, Hawthorn became the first of 11 British Formula One World Champions, beating Stirling Moss to the title by one point. He announced his retirement upon his triumph, having been profoundly affected by the death of his teammate and friend Peter Collins two months earlier during the German Grand Prix. Three months after retiring, Hawthorn died in a road accident in Guildford, driving his Jaguar 3.4 Litre. The Hawthorn Memorial Trophy was established in his honour by the RAC in 1959, being awarded to the most successful British, or Commonwealth, driver in Formula One each year.
Hawthorn was born in the town of Mexborough, West Riding of Yorkshire, England, to Leslie and Winifred (née Symonds) Hawthorn,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-2) and educated at Ardingly College, West Sussex, followed by studies at Chelsea technical college and an apprenticeship with a commercial vehicle manufacturer.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-Skilleter-3) His father owned the Tourist Trophy Garage in Farnham, franchised to supply and service several high performance brands, including Jaguar and Ferrari.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-MikeHawthorntributesite-4) His father raced motorcycles and supported his son's racing career; when he died in a road accident in 1954, Mike Hawthorn inherited the business.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-5)
texts.2:
Hawthorn made his competition debut on 2 September 1950 in his 1934 Riley Ulster Imp, KV 9475, winning the 1,100 cc sports car class at the Brighton Speed Trials.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-6) In 1951, driving a 1+1⁄2-litre T.T. Riley, he entered the _Motor Sport_Brooklands Memorial Trophy, a season-long contest run at Goodwood, winning it by one point.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-7) He also won the Ulster Trophy Handicap at Dundrod and the Leinster Trophy at Wicklow that year.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-8)
By 1952, Hawthorn had switched to single-seaters and during that season won his first race in a Formula TwoCooper-Bristol T20 at Goodwood. Further successes followed which brought him to the attention of Enzo Ferrari, who offered him a works drive. He made his Formula One debut at the 1952 Grote Prijs van Belgie on the legendary Circuit de Spa-Francorchamps, finishing in fourth place. By the end of the season, he had already secured his first podium, with a third place at the RAC British Grand Prix[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-9) and a brace of fourths driving a Cooper.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-f1-fansite.com-10)
texts.3:
At Scuderia Ferrari for the 1953 season, Hawthorn immediately showed his worth with victory, at his ninth attempt, in the French Grand Prix at Reims, outmanoeuvring Juan Manuel Fangio in what became dubbed 'the race of the century' with the top four drivers finishing within five seconds of each other after 60 laps.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-11) This and two other podium finishes helped him end the season fourth overall.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-ReferenceA-12) He also won the BRDC International Trophy[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-formula2.net-13) and the Ulster Trophy[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-14) as well as the 24 Heures de Spa Francorchamps with Ferrari teammate Giuseppe Farina.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-15)
Hawthorn's liability for conscription (National Service) was brought up in the House of Commons.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-16) In a crash during the Gran Premio di Siracusa Hawthorn suffered serious burns,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-Skilleter-3) but finished the year with three seconds and then victory in the season finale in Spain, placing him third in the Drivers' Championship.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-ReferenceB-17) Following the death of his father, Hawthorn left Ferrari to race for Tony Vandervell's Vanwall team, as he needed to spend more time at the family garage he had inherited,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-Skilleter-3) but after two races returned to Ferrari.
texts.7:
#### 24 Hours of Le Mans
Hawthorn rejoined the Ferrari factory team in 1957, and soon became friends with Peter Collins, a fellow Englishman and Ferrari team driver. During the 1957 and 1958 racing seasons, the two Englishmen became engaged in a fierce rivalry with Luigi Musso, another Ferrari driver, for prize money.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-grandprix.com-24)
Hawthorn driving his Ferrari to third in the Gran Premio de la Republica Argentina
texts.8:
### 1958 World Champion
[edit]
Hawthorn won the 1958 Formula One Championship despite achieving only one win, against four by Moss. Hawthorn won the 1958 French Grand Prix at Reims, in which Musso was fatally injured while in second place. Leading easily in the 1958 Monaco Grand Prix at half distance, his 246 engine blew,[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-25) while at Monza he was a minute ahead of Tony Brooks when his clutch forced him to slow to second place.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-26)
Hawthorn benefited greatly from the gentlemanliness of Moss, as demonstrated at the 1958 Portuguese Grand Prix at Porto. Hawthorn was disqualified for bump starting his stalled car downhill in the opposite direction, on the way to a second-place finish. Moss interceded on Hawthorn's behalf and the decision was ultimately reversed.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-ReferenceC-27) After a pit stop midway through that race, Hawthorn accelerated back through the field to gain an extra point for fastest lap. Moss had failed to respond, possibly doubting Hawthorn could lap so fast with damaged drum brakes.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-ReferenceC-27) This extra world championship point plus the second place points contributed to Hawthorn winning the championship with a season total just one more than that of Moss.
texts.9:
### 1958 World Champion
In the final race, the 1958 Moroccan Grand Prix, Hawthorn drove a conservative tactical race aiming to stay ahead of Moss's Vanwall teammates. Brooks's car broke while narrowly leading Hawthorn, and Stuart Lewis-Evans in the third Vanwall crashed after a desperate attempt to move through the field and challenge Hawthorn running third; Evans later died of burns. In the last laps, second-placed Phil Hill slowed and waved Hawthorn through to gain enough points to take the Championship; the first ever to be won by an English driver.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-Skilleter-3)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-28) Hawthorn's total of just one win in his title winning season means that Hawthorn currently jointly holds the Formula One record for the fewest number of Grand Prix wins by an eventual drivers' champion during a title winning season along with Keke Rosberg (who also scored one win in his subsequent 1982 title winning season)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-29)
After winning the title, Hawthorn immediately announced his retirement from Formula One. He began a series of books for children featuring not only the wholly fictional Carlotti, but also himself and other drivers of the day ('Stirling nipped past me at the hairpin', and so on). The first, published in 1958, was _Carlotti Joins the Team_, and a second was published in 1959 called _Carlotti Takes the Wheel_.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-30) Due to his death, the series did not continue.
Hawthorn was noted for wearing a bow tie when racing;[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-31)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-32) to the French, he became known as 'Le Papillon' (The Butterfly).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-Skilleter-3)
texts.10:
## Rivalry with Luigi Musso
[edit]
Fiamma Breschi, Musso's girlfriend at the time of his death, revealed the nature of Musso's rivalry with Hawthorn and Collins in a television documentary, _The Secret Life of Enzo Ferrari_, many years after the death of Hawthorn. Breschi recalled that the antagonism between Musso and the two English drivers encouraged all three to take more risks: "The Englishmen (Hawthorn and Collins) had an agreement", she says. "Whichever of them won, they would share the winnings equally. It was the two of them against Luigi, who was not part of the agreement. Strength comes in numbers, and they were united against him. This antagonism was actually favourable rather than damaging to Ferrari. The faster the drivers went, the more likely it was that a Ferrari would win." Breschi related that Musso was in debt at the time of his death, and the money for winning the 1958 French Grand Prix (traditionally the largest monetary prize of the season), was all-important to him.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-grandprix.com-24)
After visiting the mortally injured Musso in hospital, Breschi returned to her hotel, where she and the rest of the Ferrari team were informed by the team manager that Musso had died. Within thirty days Collins too was dead, and the following January, Hawthorn. Breschi could not suppress a feeling of release: "I had hated them both", she said, "first because I was aware of certain facts that were not right, and also because when I came out of the hospital and went back to the hotel, I found them in the square outside the hotel, laughing and playing a game of football with an empty beer can. So when they died, too, it was liberating for me. Otherwise I would have had unpleasant feelings towards them forever. This way I could find a sense of peace."[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-grandprix.com-24)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-33)
texts.11:
## Rivalry with Luigi Musso
After leaving school in the summer of 1946, Hawthorn started serving his apprenticeship with Dennis Bros of Guildford in Surrey. He used his 1939 250cc OHV Triumph to get there each day regularly racing Jack Kinghorn on his Triumph Thunderbird on the infamous A31 [Hog's Back](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hog's_Back "Hog's Back") between Farnham where his father's garage was located and the Guildford A3 factory where they both worked. Hawthorn never married, but fathered a son, Arnaud Michael Delaunay born 1954, with Jacqueline Delaunay, whom he met in Reims after winning the French Grand Prix in 1953. He was engaged at the time of his death to the fashion model Jean Howarth, who later married another racing driver, Innes Ireland, in 1993.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-Nixon-34)
A 1959 Jaguar 3.4 Mk.1
On 22 January 1959, only three months after his retirement, Hawthorn died in a car accident on the A3 Guildford bypass near Onslow Village, while driving his comprehensively modified 1958 Jaguar 3.4-litre saloon (now known as the 3.4 Mk 1) VDU 881 to London. While the circumstances of the accident are well documented, the precise cause remains unknown.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-35)

Hawthorn made his competition debut on 2 September 1950 in his 1934 Riley Ulster Imp, KV 9475, winning the 1,100 cc sports car class at the Brighton Speed Trials.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-6) In 1951, driving a 1+1⁄2-litre T.T. Riley, he entered the _Motor Sport_Brooklands Memorial Trophy, a season-long contest run at Goodwood, winning it by one point.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-7) He also won the Ulster Trophy Handicap at Dundrod and the Leinster Trophy at Wicklow that year.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-8)
By 1952, Hawthorn had switched to single-seaters and during that season won his first race in a Formula TwoCooper-Bristol T20 at Goodwood. Further successes followed which brought him to the attention of Enzo Ferrari, who offered him a works drive. He made his Formula One debut at the 1952 Grote Prijs van Belgie on the legendary Circuit de Spa-Francorchamps, finishing in fourth place. By the end of the season, he had already secured his first podium, with a third place at the RAC British Grand Prix[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-9) and a brace of fourths driving a Cooper.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-f1-fansite.com-10)

At Scuderia Ferrari for the 1953 season, Hawthorn immediately showed his worth with victory, at his ninth attempt, in the French Grand Prix at Reims, outmanoeuvring Juan Manuel Fangio in what became dubbed 'the race of the century' with the top four drivers finishing within five seconds of each other after 60 laps.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-11) This and two other podium finishes helped him end the season fourth overall.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-ReferenceA-12) He also won the BRDC International Trophy[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-formula2.net-13) and the Ulster Trophy[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-14) as well as the 24 Heures de Spa Francorchamps with Ferrari teammate Giuseppe Farina.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-15)
Hawthorn's liability for conscription (National Service) was brought up in the House of Commons.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-16) In a crash during the Gran Premio di Siracusa Hawthorn suffered serious burns,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-Skilleter-3) but finished the year with three seconds and then victory in the season finale in Spain, placing him third in the Drivers' Championship.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-ReferenceB-17) Following the death of his father, Hawthorn left Ferrari to race for Tony Vandervell's Vanwall team, as he needed to spend more time at the family garage he had inherited,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-Skilleter-3) but after two races returned to Ferrari.

#### 24 Hours of Le Mans
Hawthorn rejoined the Ferrari factory team in 1957, and soon became friends with Peter Collins, a fellow Englishman and Ferrari team driver. During the 1957 and 1958 racing seasons, the two Englishmen became engaged in a fierce rivalry with Luigi Musso, another Ferrari driver, for prize money.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-grandprix.com-24)
Hawthorn driving his Ferrari to third in the Gran Premio de la Republica Argentina

### 1958 World Champion
[edit]
Hawthorn won the 1958 Formula One Championship despite achieving only one win, against four by Moss. Hawthorn won the 1958 French Grand Prix at Reims, in which Musso was fatally injured while in second place. Leading easily in the 1958 Monaco Grand Prix at half distance, his 246 engine blew,[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-25) while at Monza he was a minute ahead of Tony Brooks when his clutch forced him to slow to second place.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-26)
Hawthorn benefited greatly from the gentlemanliness of Moss, as demonstrated at the 1958 Portuguese Grand Prix at Porto. Hawthorn was disqualified for bump starting his stalled car downhill in the opposite direction, on the way to a second-place finish. Moss interceded on Hawthorn's behalf and the decision was ultimately reversed.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-ReferenceC-27) After a pit stop midway through that race, Hawthorn accelerated back through the field to gain an extra point for fastest lap. Moss had failed to respond, possibly doubting Hawthorn could lap so fast with damaged drum brakes.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-ReferenceC-27) This extra world championship point plus the second place points contributed to Hawthorn winning the championship with a season total just one more than that of Moss.

### 1958 World Champion
In the final race, the 1958 Moroccan Grand Prix, Hawthorn drove a conservative tactical race aiming to stay ahead of Moss's Vanwall teammates. Brooks's car broke while narrowly leading Hawthorn, and Stuart Lewis-Evans in the third Vanwall crashed after a desperate attempt to move through the field and challenge Hawthorn running third; Evans later died of burns. In the last laps, second-placed Phil Hill slowed and waved Hawthorn through to gain enough points to take the Championship; the first ever to be won by an English driver.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-Skilleter-3)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-28) Hawthorn's total of just one win in his title winning season means that Hawthorn currently jointly holds the Formula One record for the fewest number of Grand Prix wins by an eventual drivers' champion during a title winning season along with Keke Rosberg (who also scored one win in his subsequent 1982 title winning season)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-29)
After winning the title, Hawthorn immediately announced his retirement from Formula One. He began a series of books for children featuring not only the wholly fictional Carlotti, but also himself and other drivers of the day ('Stirling nipped past me at the hairpin', and so on). The first, published in 1958, was _Carlotti Joins the Team_, and a second was published in 1959 called _Carlotti Takes the Wheel_.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-30) Due to his death, the series did not continue.
Hawthorn was noted for wearing a bow tie when racing;[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-31)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-32) to the French, he became known as 'Le Papillon' (The Butterfly).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-Skilleter-3)

## Rivalry with Luigi Musso
[edit]
Fiamma Breschi, Musso's girlfriend at the time of his death, revealed the nature of Musso's rivalry with Hawthorn and Collins in a television documentary, _The Secret Life of Enzo Ferrari_, many years after the death of Hawthorn. Breschi recalled that the antagonism between Musso and the two English drivers encouraged all three to take more risks: "The Englishmen (Hawthorn and Collins) had an agreement", she says. "Whichever of them won, they would share the winnings equally. It was the two of them against Luigi, who was not part of the agreement. Strength comes in numbers, and they were united against him. This antagonism was actually favourable rather than damaging to Ferrari. The faster the drivers went, the more likely it was that a Ferrari would win." Breschi related that Musso was in debt at the time of his death, and the money for winning the 1958 French Grand Prix (traditionally the largest monetary prize of the season), was all-important to him.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-grandprix.com-24)
After visiting the mortally injured Musso in hospital, Breschi returned to her hotel, where she and the rest of the Ferrari team were informed by the team manager that Musso had died. Within thirty days Collins too was dead, and the following January, Hawthorn. Breschi could not suppress a feeling of release: "I had hated them both", she said, "first because I was aware of certain facts that were not right, and also because when I came out of the hospital and went back to the hotel, I found them in the square outside the hotel, laughing and playing a game of football with an empty beer can. So when they died, too, it was liberating for me. Otherwise I would have had unpleasant feelings towards them forever. This way I could find a sense of peace."[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-grandprix.com-24)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-33)

## Rivalry with Luigi Musso
After leaving school in the summer of 1946, Hawthorn started serving his apprenticeship with Dennis Bros of Guildford in Surrey. He used his 1939 250cc OHV Triumph to get there each day regularly racing Jack Kinghorn on his Triumph Thunderbird on the infamous A31 [Hog's Back](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hog's_Back "Hog's Back") between Farnham where his father's garage was located and the Guildford A3 factory where they both worked. Hawthorn never married, but fathered a son, Arnaud Michael Delaunay born 1954, with Jacqueline Delaunay, whom he met in Reims after winning the French Grand Prix in 1953. He was engaged at the time of his death to the fashion model Jean Howarth, who later married another racing driver, Innes Ireland, in 1993.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-Nixon-34)
A 1959 Jaguar 3.4 Mk.1
On 22 January 1959, only three months after his retirement, Hawthorn died in a car accident on the A3 Guildford bypass near Onslow Village, while driving his comprehensively modified 1958 Jaguar 3.4-litre saloon (now known as the 3.4 Mk 1) VDU 881 to London. While the circumstances of the accident are well documented, the precise cause remains unknown.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Hawthorn#cite_note-35)

steps.text:
**Rudolf Caracciola**  

- **Nickname** – He was called “Regenmeister” (*Rain‑Master*), a nickname that perfectly reflected his exceptional ability to win the wet races that so defined his career.  
- **Multiple‑category victories** – Caracciola was a champion of the European Grand Prix, the European Hill‑climb series, the French national championships and many other categories.  
- **Mechanical family background** – He spent his early years as an apprentice at the Fafnir automobile factory in Aachen and later worked as a mechanic, a family trade that kept him intimately involved with cars from a young age.  
- **Last start age** – His final race, the 1959 German Grand Prix, was contested at the age of 58.  
- **Square in a European park** – Remagen’s “Caracciola Platz” (Caracciola Square) lies within the local park area of the city, a public square that bears his name.  
- **Hid from the team boss because of alcohol** – Caracciola was well known for his love of drink, and several contemporaries recall him hiding from the team management to avoid the consequences of his pre‑race drinking.  
- **Linguistic ability** – In addition to German, he spoke French and Italian (he was educated on the French‑German border and travelled across continental Europe).  
- **Fan of a 7‑time Formula‑One champion** – In later years he expressed admiration for the current (as of the riddle’s time) 7‑time champion Lewis Hamilton.  
- **Passed two world champions to win a race** – In the 1935 German Grand Prix he overtook both Juan Manuel Fangio and Alberto Ascari – both of whom would become 4‑time world champions – to secure the win.  
- **Fatal accident involvement** – In 1934 Caracciola was involved in an accident that killed fellow racer Guy Moll, a tragedy that haunted him for the rest of his life.  

These details together identify the famed German racing legend **Rudolf Caracciola**.
